lesson.title: The Event Horizon: When Outward No Longer Leads Out
lesson.objective: Explain why the event horizon is a boundary beyond which no future path—including a light beam’s—can lead back outside.
lesson.approachReason: The learner predicts what an outward-pointing laser will do, then explores light paths to discover why escape is about possible futures rather than engine power.

blocks.heading: A boundary, not a wall
blocks.body:
The event horizon is the boundary separating events that can send a signal to the distant outside universe from events that cannot. Once you are inside it, even an outward-aimed light beam cannot escape.

The horizon is not a solid shell that blocks the beam. It marks a change in which future paths are possible.
blocks.example: Think of a boundary marked on a map, not a surface made of material. Crossing it changes your escape possibilities without requiring you to hit anything.

hints: Separate a physical obstacle from a boundary between different possible paths.
Would the absence of a solid surface create an escape route?
blocks.retry: A wall stops light by interacting with it. An event horizon needs no material barrier: a light signal emitted inside simply has no future route to the distant outside universe.

blocks.heading: Why a stronger engine cannot help
blocks.body:
For the simple, nonrotating black hole we are considering, every possible future path inside the horizon leads toward smaller radius—closer to the center. Even the outward-aimed light path does so; aiming outward no longer provides a route outward.

Light still moves at the usual speed of light when measured locally. The problem is not that light becomes slow: the geometry of spacetime leaves no future path back across the horizon. A rocket or message must also follow a possible future path, so extra engine power cannot create an escape route.
blocks.example: “Outward” describes where you aim. “Escape” describes where your path eventually reaches. Inside the horizon, those are no longer the same thing.

blocks.heading: Repair the explanation
blocks.prompt: A friend says, “Light cannot escape because it gets slowed to a stop at the horizon. A stronger rocket might still get out.” Replace this with a two-sentence explanation using what you learned from the two light paths.
blocks.model: Light still travels at its usual speed when measured locally; the horizon is not a wall that stops it. Inside the horizon, no possible future path leads back outside, so neither an outward light beam nor a stronger rocket can escape.

hints: Locate the probe when each flash is emitted, rather than when the receiver detects it.
Compare the two branches of the light-path diagram.
blocks.retry: Treat each flash according to where it was emitted. Crossing later does not pull an already escaping flash back, and aiming outward does not give a flash emitted inside an escape route.

activities.title: An outward-pointing laser
activities.prompt: A probe has just crossed inside the event horizon of a simple, nonrotating black hole. It fires a laser directly away from the center. What happens to the beam?
activities.reveal: Even an outward-aimed beam cannot escape from inside the horizon. To understand why, we need to examine the paths light can take—not imagine a wall stopping it.

options.text: It escapes because it is aimed outward.
options.feedback: Aiming outward is not enough. Inside the horizon, even this light path cannot reach the outside universe.

options.text: It hits a solid shell at the horizon.
options.feedback: The horizon is not made of material. No collision with a shell is needed.

options.text: It keeps moving locally at light speed, but cannot escape.
options.feedback: Yes. Light retains its locally measured speed, but its future path cannot lead outside.

options.text: It stops moving as soon as the probe fires it.
options.feedback: A nearby observer still measures the beam moving at light speed. Failure to escape does not mean failure to move.

activities.title: Same light speed, different destinations
activities.prompt: Tap the nodes and trace both branches. Each beam is aimed directly outward and moves at the usual locally measured speed of light. Which branch can reach a distant receiver? These arrows show future paths, not a picture drawn to scale.
activities.reveal: Outside the horizon, a directly outward beam can reach a distant receiver. Inside it, even the outward-aimed beam proceeds toward smaller radius: escape is no longer among its possible futures.

nodes.label: Emission outside
nodes.detail: The probe fires while still outside the horizon of our isolated, nonrotating black hole.

nodes.label: Outward beam outside
nodes.detail: This directly outward beam travels toward larger radius. It has a route away from the black hole.

nodes.label: Distant receiver
nodes.detail: The escaping beam can reach a receiver far from the black hole.

nodes.label: Emission inside
nodes.detail: The probe fires after crossing the horizon. There is no solid surface blocking its laser.

nodes.label: Outward beam inside
nodes.detail: The beam moves locally at light speed, yet its future path does not take it back across the horizon.

nodes.label: Smaller radius
nodes.detail: Even this outward-aimed beam proceeds closer to the center. All possible future paths inside this simple black hole lead toward smaller radius.

questions.question: A mission designer says, “There is no solid surface at the event horizon, so a laser fired from inside should pass through it and escape.” What is the best correction?
options: The horizon contains an invisible material that absorbs every laser.
The absence of a solid surface does not create a future path from inside to outside.
The laser can escape if its beam is narrow enough.
Only rockets are trapped; light can always leave.
questions.correctAnswer: The absence of a solid surface does not create a future path from inside to outside.
questions.explanation: The event horizon is a boundary of escape possibilities, not a material barrier. A signal emitted inside has no future path to the distant outside universe.

questions.question: A falling probe sends flash A directly outward just before crossing the horizon, then sends flash B directly outward just after crossing. A receiver waits far away. For our isolated, nonrotating black hole, which statement is correct?
options: Both flashes can reach the receiver because both were aimed outward.
Neither flash can reach the receiver because the probe eventually crosses the horizon.
Flash A can reach the receiver, but flash B cannot, even though both move locally at light speed.
Flash B can reach the receiver if it is brighter than flash A.
questions.correctAnswer: Flash A can reach the receiver, but flash B cannot, even though both move locally at light speed.
questions.explanation: Flash A is emitted outside and has an outward escape path; the probe’s later crossing does not remove that path. Flash B is emitted inside, where no future light path leads back outside.

trace.blocks: activity > explain > check > activity > explain > reflect > check

problems: The discovery activity supplies the destinations through node labels and details, so tracing the branches mostly confirms a stated conclusion rather than letting learners discover it.
The central explanation accurately states that all future paths lead inward, but offers limited intuition for why spacetime geometry imposes this restriction.
The retry explanations largely restate the original explanation rather than providing a genuinely different explanatory route.
